title: Bank of America's $1.2B Treasury fine sparks investor class-action suit — What to do if you own stock
detail:
Bank of America's $1.2B Treasury fine sparks investor class-action suit — What to do if you own stock
Eric Esposito

BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Igor Golovniov/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

The last few months haven't been the best for Bank of America [NYSE: BAC].

Trouble for the nation's second-largest bank went mainstream this October when the U.S. Department of the Treasury alleged Bank of America (BofA) put its revenues over safety regulations with weak anti-money laundering and sanctions practices. The combined penalties levied against the bank from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Office of Foreign Assets Control totaled $1.21 billion.

According to FinCEN, BofA failed to report $5 billion in "suspicious transactions," some allegedly related to "chinese money laundering networks" and "illicit finance along the southwest border," including cartels.

At the time, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent championed these penalties, claiming, "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."​

Moneywise reached out to Bank of America for further comment. In response, a BofA spokesperson said, "Financial crime compliance is serious and we are responsible for getting it right. We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 OCC Consent Order and FinCEN's investigation.

"We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."

Senator Warren wants a Capitol Hill grilling

​Despite being the third-largest penalty ever levied by the Treasury, some lawmakers balked at the number, claiming $1.21 billion was not severe enough. Senator Elizabeth Warren, who pushed for a criminal investigation, was chief among them.​

After the news broke, Warren took to X and called the payment a "slap on the wrist." Rather than settling for these civil penalties, Warren wants BofA's executives to face the music on Capitol Hill.

As she wrote on X, "CEO Brian Moynihan owes Congress answers, and we need a criminal investigation into the apparent violation of our anti-money-laundering laws. I've long said big bank CEOs should be held personally accountable if their banks break the law."

title: Bank of America resets AMD stock price target as Nvidia CEO exits
detail:
Bank of America resets AMD stock price target as Nvidia CEO exits
Moz Farooque, Celine Provini
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 12:13 PM PST 5 min read
NVDA
BAC
AMD
AVGO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

On Nov. 12, when Nvidia (NVDA) confirmed that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had resigned, investors surprisingly didn't sell every AI chip stock.

In fact, Wall Street piled into Nvidia's biggest rivals, adding insult to injury. Nvidia stock shed 4.3% to $166.19 on Nov. 12, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) surged 5.9% to $585.30, and Broadcom (AVGO) gained 5.5%. 

Bank of America made a similar distinction in a note shared with me. Veteran analyst Vivek Arya bumped his AMD price target, cut Nvidia's, and kept a Buy rating on both.

But perhaps the more revealing number in Arya's analysis isn't the flashy new price target, but a massive new forecast for a market that tends to be overshadowed by AI accelerators.

Bank of America's $700 target starts with a different chip

Arya raised his AMD stock price target to $700 from $650 and slashed Nvidia's to $280 from $350. At the Nov. 12 close, AMD's new target implied 19.6% upside.

However, what has him reassessing his outlook on AMD is a substantial bump in his forecast for the server CPU market, which often gets overlooked amid AI GPU headlines.

He estimates the server CPU market could rise to $240 billion by 2030, up from $210 billion in his previous guidance. Interestingly, he expects AI agents to effectively drive that growth.

GPUs handle the heavy computation behind AI models, but CPUs handle work around those models, which means more AI activity drives demand for both kinds of chips.

Arya called AMD his top CPU pick, citing the breadth of its processor lineup, clock speeds, core and thread counts, and better visibility into supply. 

Speaking of processors, on Nov. 10, AMD announced general availability of its sixth-generation EPYC server processors, based on Zen 6, and said systems using them were already shipping. In fact, Microsoft Azure and Oracle had also confirmed plans to use the new chips.

AMD has already set a massive bar.

Its data-center sales skyrocketed 97% to $8.5 billion in Q3, with both EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs contributing. CEO Lisa Su told analysts on the earnings call that she expects the data-center CPU business to roughly double in 2027, according to Reuters. 

Looking ahead, AMD's Q4 outlook calls for $17 billion in companywide sales and a 55% adjusted gross margin, compared to 56% in Q3, a reminder that there's still plenty of work to be done on the margins side.

Bank of America lifts AMD's price target as Nvidia's CEO steps down.
KENT NISHIMURA / Getty Images
What AMD investors are paying for at $585

The new $700 target recovers $50 of the $70 Arya cut earlier in November. 

In that specific move, BofA has lifted its adjusted earnings estimates to $16.95 per share for 2027 and $26.14 per share for 2028, but has lowered the target from $720 to $650 as chip stock pricing multiples contracted.

title: Bank of America Flags New Risk in Asian Stocks
detail:
Bank of America Flags New Risk in Asian Stocks
Moz Farooque ACCA
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 9:19 AM PST 2 min read
BAC
TSM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Bank of America (NYSE:BAC) is flagging a risk for traders betting against Asian stocks after an AI-led selloff drew intervention from Taiwan and South Korea, according to Seeking Alpha's headline. The two markets show how quickly the trade can change when authorities step in. Government buying can lift prices, and tighter short-selling rules can make it harder to add to bearish positions.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 4 Warning Signs with BAC.

Is BAC fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

BAC GF Value chart

Taiwan authorized its NT$500 billion ($15.3 billion) National Financial Stabilization Fund to support equities after the Taiex fell 4.5% on Nov. 6. Regulators also tightened limits on short selling. The benchmark rebounded 4.9% on Nov. 9 as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) rallied. Reuters said it could not establish how much of the fund had been deployed.

South Korea took a different approach. Authorities temporarily eased a collateral requirement for brokers that make margin loans, aiming to curb forced selling. The Kospi still fell 0.8% on Nov. 9 after losing nearly 12% the previous week. The different outcomes show how much depends on the type of intervention and whether private buyers return.

Investors Takeaway

Foreign flows are one test of whether the rebound can last. Overseas investors sold about $7.7 billion of South Korean shares during the selloff week, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix accounting for most of the outflow, Reuters reported. A reversal would give the recovery broader support.

Nvidia's Nov. 17 earnings report is the next major demand test. Its data center outlook could help investors assess whether orders for advanced chips and memory are holding up. If foreign selling persists and chipmakers face weaker demand, policy support may slow the decline without changing the earnings outlook.

title: Nike is purposely selling fewer shoes as its shares keep falling
detail:
Nike is purposely selling fewer shoes as its shares keep falling
Peace Longe, Dana Sullivan Kilroy
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 10:17 AM PST 5 min read
NKE
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If you have been paying attention to Nike lately, you might have noticed that something feels off about the company's sales. Classic Jordans and other products like Air Force 1s are not appearing on store shelves the way they used to.

Their sneaker drops are also getting less attention than before. That's because Nike has intentionally restricted the supply of its classic footwear to restore scarcity and balance the market.

All this has led to a drop in Nike sales, which is showing up in the company's share price. On November 10, Nike (NKE) closed at $38.67. The stock went down 3% for the day and is roughly 40% lower this year.

That's why some Wall Street firms don't recommend buying the stock yet. Bank of America just warned investors to expect more pressure before the sneaker giant can recover.

In a BofA global research note shared with me, titled "Expect Investor Day to provide long-term optimism, but short-term caution," analyst Lorraine Hutchinson maintained her Underperform rating on Nike and kept her price target at $24. That's well below where the shares currently trade.

Why BofA still thinks Nike stock could drop further

Hutchinson has covered Nike at BofA for years. In her latest note on the stock, she cut her fiscal 2028 earnings forecast by 11% to $1.31 per share. 

Also read: AI is changing the KFC and Taco Bell experience for customers

She did that because Nike is still cleaning up Jordan Brand. The company is shipping fewer pairs to retail partners so that stores do not end up with piles of unsold boxes. The slow clean-up process is delaying the stock's recovery across more quarters, but it also protects partners like Foot Locker from heavy markdowns, Yahoo Finance reported. 

Due to the recovery delay, Hutchinson now expects Nike's sales to return to growth in the third quarter of fiscal 2028 instead of the second. 

Nike shares closed at $38.67 on Nov. 10, down about 40% so far in 2026 as Jordan Brand and lifestyle sales continue to slow.Nexpher Images / Getty Images
The lifestyle sneakers that just are not selling

Nike makes its money by selling shoes, clothing, and gear across performance sports like running and basketball. The company also has a large lifestyle business built on Jordan and classic silhouettes. That lifestyle side is where the business is hurting.

On Nike's first-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call transcribed by MarketBeat on Oct. 1, CEO Elliott Hill said Jordan Brand revenue fell by a mid-teens rate during the quarter. He also said that older Sportswear shoes had been stuck on store shelves for too long.

title: Peter Schiff Warns Banks Hold “$2 Trillion in Mortgage Losses” as the 10-Year Nears 5%
detail:
Peter Schiff Warns Banks Hold “$2 Trillion in Mortgage Losses” as the 10-Year Nears 5%
Gian Estrada
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 7:20 AM PST 4 min read
JPM
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Peter Schiff Warns Banks Hold "$2 Trillion in Mortgage Losses" as the 10-Year Nears 5% ©PeterPhoto from Getty Images Signature, Warchi from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Peter Schiff says banks hold $2 trillion of unrealized mortgage losses as the 10-year yield nears 5%.

Bank of America's paper losses topped $109 billion, and its capital is the pressure point.

JPMorgan trades near its high multiple of tangible book.

The 10-year Treasury yield is back near 5% after a hot inflation report on Nov. 10, and Peter Schiff says that's a bigger problem for banks than it looks. Big holders of low-rate mortgage bonds like Bank of America (BAC:NYSE) feel it first, and it tests how much bad news JPMorgan Chase (JPM:NYSE) holders have priced in.

Schiff, chief economist at Euro Pacific Asset Management, posted on X that banks have "$2 Trillion in Mortgage Losses." Then he added: "The banks are losing money on 100% of their mortgages, even if not one of them defaults."

Schiff's Number Is Six Times the FDIC's

The FDIC put banks' unrealized losses on securities at $326.7 billion at the end of June, about a sixth of Schiff's figure. But Schiff is talking about mortgages overall, not just the bonds in banks' securities portfolios, so the two numbers aren't directly comparable. A 3% mortgage is worth less when the 10-year pays 5%, even without a missed payment.

Bank of America's unrealized losses on debt securities topped $109 billion in the third quarter, up 28% from the end of June, according to its filings. Most of those bonds are held to maturity, so their losses don't touch book value unless sold. Tangible book value per share rose 3% in a year, to $29.14.

The stock trades at 1.7x tangible book, close to its five-year average of 1.6x. It bottomed at 1.1x in October 2023, when these losses topped $131 billion:

BAC Stock Price/Tangible Book Value: 5-Year (TIKR)
The Losses Come Due as Lost Income

The real cost is the income Bank of America gave up by locking in low yields, and it shrinks as those bonds pay off. Management said in January that $12 billion to $15 billion of mortgage securities and loans would roll off each quarter this year, allowing reinvestment at yields 150 to 200 basis points higher or repayment of expensive short-term debt. Net interest income rose 8% in the third quarter, to $16.4 billion.

Total revenue grew from $92.4 billion in 2022 to $107 billion in 2025:

title: Wall Street Divided on S&P 500: Which ETFs Could Benefit in 2027?
detail:
Wall Street Divided on S&P 500: Which ETFs Could Benefit in 2027?

The outlook for the S&P 500 in 2027 is becoming increasingly divided, with Wall Street strategists weighing the possibility of another strong rally against concerns about elevated equity exposure, artificial intelligence (AI) valuations, rising borrowing costs and geopolitical uncertainty.

While UBS remains optimistic about the benchmark, forecasting that the S&P 500 could reach 8,900 by the end of 2027, Bank of America (BofA) has adopted a more cautious stance. The contrasting outlooks raise an important question for investors.

For ETF investors, the answer could influence not only broad-market funds tracking the S&P 500 but also its inverse ETFs too.

Performance of S&P 500 in 2026: A Year of Gains & Volatility

The S&P 500 has delivered positive returns so far in 2026, although its performance has been accompanied by considerable volatility.

As of Nov. 12, 2026, the index closed at 7,592.40, representing a gain of 10.9% from the start of the year. It had reached a record closing high of 7,818.93 on Oct. 6 before retreating amid concerns surrounding AI-related valuations, higher oil prices and geopolitical developments.

The mid-term election results also influenced market sentiment, with Democrats gaining control of both chambers of Congress. The outcome initially eased political uncertainty and helped lift the S&P 500 1.6% on Nov. 4, 2026. However, the index plunged 4.4% on Nov. 5 as concerns over potential AI regulation, data-center restrictions and technology-sector valuations triggered a broad sell-off, erasing the previous day's gains and highlighting market volatility.

Why Does UBS Expect the S&P 500 to Reach 8,900?

UBS has maintained its 2027-end target of 8,900 for the S&P 500, suggesting an upside of 17.22% from the Nov. 12 closing level.

According to UBS strategist Keith Parker, as quoted in an Investing.com article and cited by Yahoo Finance, the bank noted that the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio declined approximately 20% in 2026, even as earnings remained on track for substantial growth.

UBS expects earnings per share of the S&P 500 to increase 18% year over year to $430 in 2027 and share buybacks to recover by $200-$400 billion next year, per the above-mentioned article.

However, UBS also acknowledged that concerns about AI investment returns, higher Treasury yields, widening credit spreads, rising oil prices and the possibility of state-level restrictions on data center construction following the mid-term elections remain key risks.
